steps.title: Key Fact
steps.body: The English legal system is based on common law (judge-made law) and statute law (Acts of Parliament)

steps.title: Key Fact
steps.body: Parliament is the supreme law-making body — parliamentary sovereignty means no Parliament can bind its successors

steps.title: Key Fact
steps.body: The court hierarchy ensures that lower courts follow the decisions of higher courts (doctrine of precedent)

steps.title: Key Fact
steps.body: The Supreme Court is the highest court in the UK for civil and criminal matters

steps.title: Try it yourself
steps.body: Q: What is the difference between common law and statute law? | Q: Why is parliamentary sovereignty important? | Q: What is the doctrine of precedent?

steps.title: Check your answers
steps.body: Common law is judge-made law developed through court decisions over centuries; statute law is written law made by Parliament through Acts. | It means Parliament is the supreme law-making body — its laws cannot be overridden by courts or other bodies, and no Parliament can bind a future Parliament. | Courts must follow decisions made by higher courts in similar cases. This ensures consistency and predictability in the law.

steps.title: Exam tips
steps.body: Know the difference between common law and statute law — both are sources of law Parliamentary sovereignty is a key concept — be able to explain and evaluate it The court hierarchy is essential knowledge — know which courts hear which cases Use specific examples of legal personnel and their roles Legal aid is often examined as a contemporary issue — know its scope and limitations
